name: Seraiah
source_summary: A royal quartermaster and brother of Jeremiah's scribe Baruch, sent by Jeremiah to Babylon with a written scroll of judgment against the city, which he was to read aloud and then sink in the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon would fall and never rise again.
family_friendly_summary: Seraiah held an important job serving King Zedekiah, and one time he traveled with the king all the way to Babylon. Before he left, the prophet Jeremiah gave him a scroll with a written message about all the bad things that would eventually happen to Babylon, the powerful empire that had been troubling Judah. Jeremiah told Seraiah to read the scroll out loud once he got to Babylon, then tie a stone to it and throw it into the river, saying that Babylon would sink down just like the scroll and never rise again. Seraiah's simple act of obedience carried a huge message of hope for God's people.
adult_story: Seraiah, son of Neriah and brother of Jeremiah's scribe Baruch, served as chief quartermaster for King Zedekiah of Judah. When Zedekiah traveled to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign, Jeremiah entrusted Seraiah with a written scroll recording "all the evil that would come upon Babylon" -- every word of judgment the prophet had spoken against the empire that would soon destroy Jerusalem (Jeremiah 51:59-60). Jeremiah gave Seraiah precise instructions: read the entire scroll aloud once he arrived in Babylon, pray over it acknowledging that the LORD Himself had spoken this judgment, then tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the Euphrates, declaring, "Thus Babylon will sink down and not rise again because of the calamity that I am going to bring upon her" (51:61-64). The act was a piece of prophetic street theater performed at the very heart of the empire Judah feared -- a small, deliberate act of faith proclaiming, in the capital of the world's greatest power, that its fall was already certain in God's plan. Seraiah's obedience carried Jeremiah's message of judgment on Babylon and hope for God's exiled people into enemy territory itself.
